## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- declare and define **functions** in C and C++, explain **pass by value**,
  use pointers to return several results, and describe what happens on the
  **call stack**;
- distinguish the **scope** and the **lifetime** of variables (local, global,
  `static`);
- use the three **standard streams** — `stdin`, `stdout`, `stderr` — from C
  (`<stdio.h>`) and C++ (`<iostream>`), and explain **buffering**, with a
  **proof** of how many system calls it saves;
- read **user input robustly**: explain why `scanf` and `cin >> x` are
  fragile, parse numbers with full error checking, and **prove** the overflow
  test used by every correct integer parser;
- **read and write files** in C (`fopen`, `fgets`, `fprintf`, `fclose`) and in
  C++ (`std::ifstream`, `std::ofstream`), handle missing files and errors, and
  write a CSV encoder/decoder that survives commas and quotes in the data.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
Functions; reading input from the user; accessing files — in C and C++.
:::

## Intuition: workshops, conveyor belts and a filing cabinet

A **function** is a workshop with a door for materials (the parameters) and a
door for the product (the return value): the rest of the program does not need
to know what happens inside (@sec-ch-functions). In C the workshop receives
**copies** of the materials — what happens to them inside never affects the
originals — unless you hand over the *address* of the original
(@sec-pointers).

A program talks to the outside world through **streams**: conveyor belts of
bytes. Three are always there: one from the keyboard (**standard input**), one
to the screen (**standard output**), and one for error messages (**standard
error**). A **file** is a stream whose other end is a drawer of the filing
cabinet: the data stay there after the program ends (@sec-ch-files).

The hard part is not the mechanics but **distrust**: users type letters where
numbers are expected, files go missing or contain garbage. A program for
non-technical users must treat every byte that comes from outside as
potentially wrong.

## Functions in C and C++ {#sec-c-functions}

### Declaration, definition, call

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>

double celsius_to_fahrenheit(double c);      /* declaration (prototype): name, parameters, result */

int main(void)
{
    for (int c = -10; c <= 40; c += 25)
        printf("%3d C = %5.1f F\n", c, celsius_to_fahrenheit(c));   /* the int is converted to double */
    return 0;
}

double celsius_to_fahrenheit(double c)       /* definition: the body */
{
    return c * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0;
}
""", name="functions.c")
```

A function has a **return type** (`void` if it returns nothing), a name, and a
list of **typed parameters**. The compiler checks every call against the
declaration: number and types of arguments (converting them when allowed, as
`int` → `double` above) and use of the result. This is why a function must be
declared before it is called, and why declarations go in headers
(@sec-multifile). In C, an empty parameter list should be written `(void)`; in
C++ `()` already means "no parameters".

### Pass by value

C passes every argument **by value**: the parameter is a new local variable
initialised with a copy of the argument.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>

void try_to_reset(int x)      { x = 0; }          /* changes its own copy */
void reset(int *x)            { *x = 0; }         /* changes the caller's variable through its address */

void min_max(const int *a, int n, int *min, int *max)   /* two results: two out-parameters */
{
    *min = *max = a[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
        if (a[i] < *min) *min = a[i];
        if (a[i] > *max) *max = a[i];
    }
}

int main(void)
{
    int value = 42;
    try_to_reset(value);
    printf("after try_to_reset: %d\n", value);
    reset(&value);
    printf("after reset(&value): %d\n", value);

    int data[] = {7, -2, 19, 4}, lo, hi;
    min_max(data, 4, &lo, &hi);
    printf("min = %d, max = %d\n", lo, hi);
    return 0;
}
""", name="byvalue.c")
```

(GCC even warns that the assignment in `try_to_reset` is useless: the
parameter is set but never used again.) Three idioms follow:

- to let a function **modify** a variable, pass its **address** (`reset(&value)`);
- to return **several results**, use **out-parameters** (pointers to the
  caller's variables), or return a `struct` (@sec-ch-c-vs-cpp);
- to pass a **large object** without copying it, pass a pointer — marked
  `const` if the function must not modify it (`const int *a`): the compiler
  then rejects any write through it.

C++ adds **references**, which make the last two idioms safer and lighter
(@sec-ch-c-vs-cpp). Python's model, "pass by object reference" (@sec-arguments),
sits between the two: the function receives a reference to the same object,
but rebinding the parameter does not affect the caller.

### The call stack {#sec-call-stack}

Each call creates an **activation record** (a *stack frame*) on the **call
stack**: room for the parameters, the local variables and the address to
return to. The frame is destroyed when the function returns — which is why a
function must never return the address of one of its local variables: the
pointer would **dangle** (@sec-malloc).

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>

unsigned long long factorial(unsigned n)
{
    int local;                                         /* lives in this call's frame */
    printf("%*sfactorial(%u): frame at %p\n", (int)(10 - n) * 2, "", n, (void *)&local);
    return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * factorial(n - 1);          /* each recursive call: a new frame */
}

int main(void)
{
    printf("5! = %llu\n", factorial(5));
    return 0;
}
""", name="stack.c", flags=("-O0",))
```

The addresses **decrease** by a fixed amount at each call (64 bytes here): on
x86-64 the stack
grows towards lower addresses, and each frame of `factorial` occupies the same
number of bytes. Recursion depth is therefore limited by the size of the stack
(typically 8 MiB on Linux, 1 MiB on Windows): a recursion a million calls deep
**overflows the stack** and crashes. Python protects you with a recursion limit
(@sec-recursion); C and C++ do not.

### Scope and lifetime

Two different questions are asked about a variable:

| | **Scope**: where is the name visible? | **Lifetime**: when does the object exist? |
|---|---|---|
| local variable | the block `{ … }` where it is declared | from its declaration to the end of the block (automatic storage) |
| `static` local variable | the block | the whole run of the program (initialised once) |
| global variable | the file (and other files, if declared `extern` there) | the whole run |
| `static` global / function | this file only (internal linkage) | the whole run |
| `malloc`/`new` memory | — (reached through pointers) | until `free`/`delete` |

: Scope and lifetime in C and C++ {#tbl-scope-lifetime}

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>

static int calls_total = 0;          /* global, visible in this file only */

int next_id(void)
{
    static int last = 1000;          /* initialised once, keeps its value between calls */
    ++calls_total;
    return ++last;
}

int main(void)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i)
        printf("new id: %d\n", next_id());
    printf("next_id was called %d times\n", calls_total);
    return 0;
}
""", name="static.c")
```

Global mutable variables make programs hard to reason about (any function may
change them) and hard to test; the CRM keeps all its state inside objects
(@sec-ch-cpp-oop).

## Standard streams and buffering {#sec-streams}

Every process starts with three open streams, numbered 0, 1, 2 by the
operating system (they are its first three **file descriptors**):

| Stream | C (`<stdio.h>`) | C++ (`<iostream>`) | Descriptor | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| standard input | `stdin` | `std::cin` | 0 | keyboard |
| standard output | `stdout` | `std::cout` | 1 | terminal |
| standard error | `stderr` | `std::cerr` | 2 | terminal |

: The three standard streams {#tbl-std-streams}

Normal results go to standard output, diagnostics to standard error. The
distinction matters as soon as the output is **redirected** (`./prog > out.txt`)
or **piped** into another program (`./prog | sort`): errors still reach the
user instead of corrupting the data. @sec-ch-cpp-python builds on exactly this.

### Buffering {#sec-buffering}

Writing to a file or terminal is ultimately done by the operating system
through a **system call** (`write` on Unix), which is expensive compared with
copying a few bytes in memory. The C and C++ libraries therefore **buffer**
output: `printf` copies the text into an array in memory, and the library calls
`write` only when the buffer is full, when the stream is closed or explicitly
flushed (`fflush`, `std::flush`, `std::endl`), or — for an interactive terminal
— at each newline.

::: {#prp-buffering}
## System calls saved by buffering
Writing a total of $n$ bytes through a buffer of $B$ bytes, with no explicit
flushes, performs at most $\lceil n/B \rceil$ write system calls; writing the
same data in $k$ unbuffered pieces performs $k$ system calls.
:::

*In one line:* each system call of a buffered stream carries a full buffer,
except possibly the last.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-buffering
The library issues a write only when the buffer is full ($B$ bytes) or at the
final close (between 1 and $B$ bytes, if any remain). If $w$ writes happen,
the first $w - 1$ carry exactly $B$ bytes, so $(w - 1)B < n$, i.e.
$w < n/B + 1$, hence $w \le \lceil n/B\rceil$. (Libraries that write large
pieces directly, bypassing the buffer, only reduce $w$.) Unbuffered, every
piece is written by its own call. $\blacksquare$
:::

We can count the system calls with `strace`, which traces the calls a program
makes to the Linux kernel. The program writes 10 000 short lines, first with
the default buffering of a file, then with buffering disabled:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

int main(int argc, char **argv)
{
    FILE *f = fopen("lines.txt", "w");
    if (f == NULL) { perror("lines.txt"); return 1; }
    if (argc > 1 && strcmp(argv[1], "unbuffered") == 0)
        setvbuf(f, NULL, _IONBF, 0);                 /* disable buffering for this stream */
    for (int i = 0; i < 10000; ++i)
        fprintf(f, "line %d\n", i);
    fclose(f);
    return 0;
}
""", name="buffering.c", run_it=False)
sh("strace -c -e trace=write ./buffering 2>&1 | grep -E 'calls|write$' ; "
   "strace -c -e trace=write ./buffering unbuffered 2>&1 | grep -E 'write$'; wc -c lines.txt")
```

98 890 bytes through a 4 096-byte buffer: $\lceil 98\,890 / 4\,096 \rceil = 25$
system calls, exactly as @prp-buffering predicts, against 10 000. The flip side
of buffering: output still in the buffer is **lost if the program crashes**,
and output to a pipe may appear later than you expect. That is why `stderr` is
unbuffered, and why a program that talks to another program through a pipe must
flush at the right moments (@sec-ch-cpp-python). In C++, prefer `'\n'` to
`std::endl` in loops: `std::endl` flushes every time.

## Reading user input robustly {#sec-robust-input}

### Why `scanf("%d")` and `cin >> n` are fragile

`scanf("%d", &n)` reads characters that form an integer and **stops at the
first character that does not fit**, leaving it in the input. If the user
types `abc`, nothing is consumed, `n` is not assigned, and `scanf` returns 0 —
a program that ignores the return value uses garbage, and a program that loops
"until valid" loops forever on the same `abc`:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int n = -1;
    for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= 4; ++attempt) {      /* bounded, so that the demo ends */
        int ok = scanf("%d", &n);
        printf("attempt %d: scanf returned %d, n = %d\n", attempt, ok, n);
        if (ok == 1) break;
    }
    return 0;
}
""", name="scanf_trap.c", stdin="abc\n12\n")
```

The `12` on the second line is never reached: `abc` blocks the input forever.
C++'s `std::cin >> n` has the same behaviour plus a **failure state**: after a
failed extraction the stream ignores every later operation until you call
`std::cin.clear()` — and `abc` is still waiting in the input. Other problems
are subtler: `scanf("%d")` accepts `12abc` (it reads `12` and leaves `abc`),
gives undefined behaviour on numbers that do not fit in an `int`, and mixing
`>>` with line-oriented reading leaves stray newlines behind.

### A robust recipe: read a line, then parse it

The reliable pattern, in both C and C++, separates two steps:

1. **read a whole line** as text (`fgets` in C, `std::getline` in C++) — this
   always consumes the user's input, whatever it is, and detects end of input;
2. **parse** the text with a function that reports *precisely* whether it is a
   valid value: all characters used, no overflow, within the allowed range.

Every integer parser, from `strtol` to Python's `int()`, builds the value digit
by digit with Horner's rule ($v \leftarrow 10v + d$, @sec-bits) and must stop
**before** the value overflows. The test it uses deserves a proof:

::: {#prp-overflow-test}
## Detecting overflow before it happens
Let $M \ge 9$ be the largest representable value and $0 \le d \le 9$ a digit.
For every integer $v \ge 0$,
$$
10v + d \le M \iff v \le \left\lfloor \frac{M - d}{10} \right\rfloor .
$$
The right-hand side is computed without overflow, so the parser can test it
**before** computing $10v + d$.
:::

*In one line:* move the operation to the other side of the inequality, where
the numbers only get smaller.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-overflow-test
$10v + d \le M \iff 10 v \le M - d \iff v \le (M - d)/10$, dividing by the
positive number 10. Since $v$ is an integer, $v \le x \iff v \le \lfloor x\rfloor$
for any real $x$ (if $v \le x$ then $v$ is an integer not exceeding $x$, hence
not exceeding the largest such integer $\lfloor x\rfloor$; the converse is
immediate). Finally $0 \le M - d \le M$, so $M - d$ and its quotient by 10 are
representable. $\blacksquare$
:::

Here is the recipe in C with the standard `strtol` ("string to long"), which
implements that test and reports overflow through `errno`:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <errno.h>
#include <limits.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Parse text as an int in [lo, hi]. Returns true and stores the value on success. */
bool parse_int(const char *text, int lo, int hi, int *out)
{
    char *end;
    errno = 0;
    long v = strtol(text, &end, 10);          /* end: first character NOT used */
    if (end == text) return false;            /* no digits at all */
    while (*end == ' ' || *end == '\t' || *end == '\n') ++end;
    if (*end != '\0') return false;           /* trailing garbage, e.g. "12abc" */
    if (errno == ERANGE) return false;        /* did not fit in a long */
    if (v < lo || v > hi) return false;       /* outside the allowed range */
    *out = (int)v;
    return true;
}

int main(void)
{
    char line[128];
    int age;
    for (;;) {
        printf("Age (0-130): ");
        if (fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin) == NULL) {     /* end of input (Ctrl+D / Ctrl+Z) */
            printf("\nNo more input.\n");
            return 1;
        }
        printf("%s", line);                                /* echo, to show the transcript */
        if (parse_int(line, 0, 130, &age)) break;
        printf("  '%.*s' is not a whole number between 0 and 130.\n",
               (int)strcspn(line, "\n"), line);
    }
    printf("Age accepted: %d\n", age);
    return 0;
}
""", name="robust.c", stdin="abc\n12abc\n99999999999999999999\n-5\n  42  \n")
```

Five inputs, four of them wrong in different ways, and the program neither
crashes nor loops: each line is consumed, judged and either accepted or
explained.

### The same in C++ {#sec-cpp-input}

C++17 added `std::from_chars` (header `<charconv>`), a fast parser that never
throws, does not depend on the locale, and reports exactly how many characters
it used and whether the value was out of range. Combined with `std::getline`
it gives a compact, robust reader — this is the code the CRM uses:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <charconv>
#include <iostream>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

// Remove spaces and tabs at both ends.
std::string_view trim(std::string_view s) {
    const auto first = s.find_first_not_of(" \t\r");
    if (first == std::string_view::npos) return {};
    const auto last = s.find_last_not_of(" \t\r");
    return s.substr(first, last - first + 1);
}

// The whole text must be an integer in [lo, hi]; otherwise: no value.
std::optional<int> parse_int(std::string_view text, int lo, int hi) {
    text = trim(text);
    int value{};
    const auto [ptr, ec] = std::from_chars(text.data(), text.data() + text.size(), value);
    if (ec != std::errc{} || ptr != text.data() + text.size() || text.empty())
        return std::nullopt;                         // not a number, trailing junk, or out of int range
    if (value < lo || value > hi) return std::nullopt;
    return value;
}

// Ask until the answer is valid; std::nullopt if the input ends.
std::optional<int> ask_int(std::istream& in, std::ostream& out,
                           const std::string& prompt, int lo, int hi) {
    std::string line;
    while (true) {
        out << prompt;
        if (!std::getline(in, line)) return std::nullopt;     // end of input
        out << line << '\n';                                  // echo (for the transcript)
        if (auto v = parse_int(line, lo, hi)) return v;
        out << "  Please type a whole number between " << lo << " and " << hi << ".\n";
    }
}

int main() {
    while (auto choice = ask_int(std::cin, std::cout, "Menu option (0-4): ", 0, 4)) {
        std::cout << "  -> option " << *choice << '\n';
        if (*choice == 0) break;
    }
    std::cout << "Bye.\n";
}
""", name="robust.cpp", stdin="2\nfour\n\n7\n3 \n0\n")
```

Three C++ types appear here and will return in @sec-ch-c-vs-cpp:
`std::string` (a string that owns its characters and knows its length),
`std::string_view` (a cheap, non-owning view of characters stored elsewhere)
and `std::optional<int>` (either an `int` or *nothing* — a type-safe way to say
"no valid value", where C needs an out-parameter plus a `bool`). Reading
functions receive the streams as parameters (`std::istream& in`) rather than
using `std::cin` directly: in the project this lets us test the user interface
with scripted input, exactly as Part I did with an injected `input` function
(@sec-ch-project-phonebook).

## Files {#sec-c-files}

### Files in C

A file is opened with `fopen(path, mode)`, which returns a `FILE *` — or `NULL`
on failure, with the reason in `errno`. The mode is `"r"` (read), `"w"`
(write, **truncating** an existing file), or `"a"` (append), optionally with
`"b"` for binary files (@tbl-open-modes is the same idea in Python). Reading
and writing use the same functions as the standard streams, with an `f` in
front: `fprintf`, `fgets`, `fputs`, `fscanf`; `fclose` flushes and closes.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

int main(void)
{
    FILE *out = fopen("scores.txt", "w");
    if (out == NULL) { perror("scores.txt"); return 1; }
    fprintf(out, "Ada 93\nAlan 88\nGrace 97\n");
    if (fclose(out) != 0) { perror("closing scores.txt"); return 1; }   /* a write error may appear only here */

    FILE *in = fopen("scores.txt", "r");
    if (in == NULL) { perror("scores.txt"); return 1; }
    char name[64];
    int score, total = 0, count = 0;
    while (fscanf(in, "%63s %d", name, &score) == 2) {   /* %63s: never more than the buffer holds */
        printf("%-6s %3d\n", name, score);
        total += score;
        ++count;
    }
    fclose(in);
    printf("average: %.1f\n", count ? (double)total / count : 0.0);

    FILE *missing = fopen("no_such_file.txt", "r");
    if (missing == NULL) {
        fflush(stdout);                                  /* keep the on-screen order (see buffering) */
        perror("no_such_file.txt");                      /* prints the reason, from errno, on stderr */
    }
    return 0;
}
""", name="files.c")
```

`perror` prints our message followed by the system's description of `errno`
(here "No such file or directory") on **standard error**. Two details are easy
to miss: write errors (disk full) may surface only at `fclose`, so its result
must be checked too; and on Windows, text mode translates `"\n"` to `"\r\n"`
on output and back on input, while binary mode (`"rb"`, `"wb"`) does not —
always use binary mode for non-text data (@sec-text-vs-binary).

### Files in C++

C++ wraps files in **stream objects**: `std::ifstream` (input), `std::ofstream`
(output) and `std::fstream` (both), in `<fstream>`. They work exactly like
`std::cin` and `std::cout`, and they **close themselves** when the object goes
out of scope — the RAII principle of @sec-ch-cpp-oop, the C++ counterpart of
Python's `with` (@sec-context-managers).

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <fstream>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    {
        std::ofstream out("notes.txt");               // opens (and truncates) for writing
        if (!out) { std::cerr << "cannot create notes.txt\n"; return 1; }
        out << "first line\n" << "second line\n";
    }                                                 // out is destroyed here: flushed and closed

    std::ifstream in("notes.txt");
    if (!in) { std::cerr << "cannot open notes.txt\n"; return 1; }
    std::string line;
    int number = 0;
    while (std::getline(in, line))                    // false at end of file (or on error)
        std::cout << ++number << ": " << line << '\n';

    std::ifstream missing("missing.txt");
    std::cout << "missing.txt opened? " << std::boolalpha << missing.is_open() << '\n';
}
""", name="files.cpp")
```

### A CSV format that survives real data {#sec-csv-cpp}

The project stores customers in a **CSV** file: one record per line, fields
separated by a delimiter. What if a field *contains* the delimiter — an address
like `Via Roma 1, Milano` — or a quote, or a newline? RFC 4180 answers
[@rfc4180]: enclose such a field in double quotes and double every quote inside
it. In @prp-csv-roundtrip we proved that this encoding can always be decoded
back to the original fields. Here is an implementation in C++ that the CRM
reuses:

```{python}
code_csv = r"""
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

// Encode one field: quote it if it contains a comma, a quote or a line break.
std::string csv_escape(const std::string& field) {
    if (field.find_first_of(",\"\r\n") == std::string::npos) return field;
    std::string out = "\"";
    for (char c : field) {
        if (c == '"') out += '"';              // a quote is written twice
        out += c;
    }
    return out + '"';
}

std::string csv_join(const std::vector<std::string>& fields) {
    std::string line;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < fields.size(); ++i) {
        if (i > 0) line += ',';
        line += csv_escape(fields[i]);
    }
    return line;
}

// Decode one record (a line without line breaks inside fields). Returns false if malformed.
bool csv_split(const std::string& line, std::vector<std::string>& fields) {
    fields.assign(1, "");
    bool quoted = false;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < line.size(); ++i) {
        const char c = line[i];
        if (quoted) {
            if (c == '"' && i + 1 < line.size() && line[i + 1] == '"') { fields.back() += '"'; ++i; }
            else if (c == '"') quoted = false;            // closing quote
            else fields.back() += c;
        } else if (c == '"' && fields.back().empty()) {
            quoted = true;                                // opening quote at the start of a field
        } else if (c == ',') {
            fields.emplace_back();                        // next field
        } else {
            fields.back() += c;
        }
    }
    return !quoted;                                       // an unclosed quote is an error
}

int main() {
    const std::vector<std::string> record = {"42", "Rossi", "Via Roma 1, Milano", "He said \"yes\"", ""};
    const std::string line = csv_join(record);
    std::cout << "encoded: " << line << '\n';
    std::vector<std::string> back;
    std::cout << "decoded ok: " << std::boolalpha << csv_split(line, back) << '\n';
    for (const auto& f : back) std::cout << "  [" << f << "]\n";
    std::cout << "round trip exact: " << (back == record) << '\n';
    std::cout << "malformed line accepted? " << csv_split("1,\"unterminated", back) << '\n';
}
"""
run(code_csv, name="csv.cpp")
```

The decoder is a tiny **state machine** with two states (inside or outside
quotes), the same structure as the proof of @prp-csv-roundtrip; it rejects an
unterminated quote instead of guessing. (To keep the format line-oriented, the
CRM also refuses line breaks inside fields when they are typed — a simple
validation rule is often better than a more general parser.)

## Practice: a report from a data file {#sec-report-example}

Putting the chapter together: a C++ program that reads policies from a CSV
file, skips and reports malformed lines (with their line number, on standard
error), and prints a summary — the robust-loading pattern of the project.

```{python}
write("policies.csv", '''id,customer,product,premium_cents
1,Rossi,car,48000
2,"Bianchi, Anna",home,21050
3,Verdi,life,not-a-number
4,Neri,car
5,Esposito,home,19900
''')
main_report = r"""
// report.cpp — csv_escape, csv_join and csv_split as above, plus:
#include <charconv>
#include <fstream>
#include <map>

int main() {
    std::ifstream in("policies.csv");
    if (!in) { std::cerr << "policies.csv not found\n"; return 1; }
    std::string line;
    std::getline(in, line);                                    // skip the header
    std::map<std::string, long long> premium_by_product;       // kept sorted by key
    int line_no = 1, good = 0;
    std::vector<std::string> f;
    while (std::getline(in, line)) {
        ++line_no;
        long long cents = 0;
        bool ok = csv_split(line, f) && f.size() == 4;
        if (ok) {
            const std::string& p = f[3];
            auto [ptr, ec] = std::from_chars(p.data(), p.data() + p.size(), cents);
            ok = ec == std::errc{} && ptr == p.data() + p.size() && cents >= 0;
        }
        if (!ok) { std::cerr << "line " << line_no << " skipped: " << line << '\n'; continue; }
        premium_by_product[f[2]] += cents;
        ++good;
    }
    std::cout << good << " valid policies\n";
    for (const auto& [product, cents] : premium_by_product)
        std::cout << "  " << product << ": " << cents / 100 << '.'
                  << (cents % 100 < 10 ? "0" : "") << cents % 100 << " EUR\n";
}
"""
show(main_report)
write("report.cpp", code_csv.split("int main()")[0] + main_report)
compile_sources(["report.cpp"], "report")
run_exe("report")
```

The input file contains a quoted name with a comma, a premium that is not a
number and a line with a missing field. The two diagnostics, written on
unbuffered standard error, appear *before* the report, which standard output
kept in its buffer until the program ended (@sec-buffering). Money is kept in **integer cents** (@sec-c-floats) and printed by integer
division and remainder.

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** Three requirements of the CRM (@sec-crm-brief) are built
from this chapter. **R8** (persistence): customers and interactions are saved to
CSV files with the escaping of @sec-csv-cpp and loaded automatically at start;
a missing file means "first run, empty CRM", and malformed lines are skipped
and reported with their line number, as in @sec-report-example. **R11** (robust
input): every value typed by the user goes through `std::getline` and a
validating parser (`ask_choice`, `ask_text`, `ask_date`, `ask_money`), which re-asks with a
clear message and treats end of input as "quit and save" — never as a crash.
And the reading functions take `std::istream&`/`std::ostream&` parameters, so
that the whole user interface can be driven by a script in the tests
(@sec-ch-cpp-python).
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Expecting a function to modify its argument**: C copies arguments; pass a
  pointer (or, in C++, a reference).
- **Returning the address of a local variable**: it dangles after the return.
- **Ignoring return values**: `scanf`, `fopen`, `fclose`, `strtol`'s `end`
  pointer — every one of them reports failures you must check.
- **`scanf("%d")` / `cin >> n` on user input**: invalid text blocks the input
  or puts the stream in a failure state. Read lines, then parse.
- **`%s` without a width** in `scanf`: a buffer overflow (@sec-c-strings).
- **`atoi`**: returns 0 for invalid input, indistinguishable from a real 0. Use
  `strtol` or `std::from_chars`.
- **Forgetting to flush** before waiting for input from another program; or,
  conversely, `std::endl` in hot loops.
- **Mode `"w"` on the file you meant to read**: it truncates it to zero bytes.
- **Text mode for binary data on Windows**: `\n` bytes are altered.
:::

## Summary

- Functions are declared (prototype) and defined; the compiler checks every
  call. Arguments are passed **by value**; pointers let a function modify the
  caller's variables or return several results; `const` documents read-only
  access.
- Each call has a **stack frame**; frames vanish on return (never return
  addresses of locals); deep recursion overflows the stack.
- **Scope** (where a name is visible) and **lifetime** (when the object exists)
  differ for locals, `static` locals, globals and heap memory.
- The three **standard streams** are `stdin`/`cin`, `stdout`/`cout`,
  `stderr`/`cerr`. Output is **buffered**: at most $\lceil n/B\rceil$ system
  calls for $n$ bytes (@prp-buffering).
- **Robust input** = read a whole line, then parse it completely and check the
  range. Parsers detect overflow *before* it happens with
  $v \le \lfloor (M-d)/10\rfloor$ (@prp-overflow-test). In C: `fgets` +
  `strtol`; in C++: `std::getline` + `std::from_chars` + `std::optional`.
- **Files**: `fopen`/`fclose` and the `f…` functions in C, checking `NULL` and
  `errno`; `std::ifstream`/`std::ofstream` in C++, which close automatically.
  CSV fields containing commas or quotes must be quoted (RFC 4180).

## Exercises

::: {#exr-cpp5-swap}
Write a C function `swap(int *a, int *b)` that exchanges two integers, and
explain why `void swap(int a, int b)` cannot work. What does the call
`swap(&x, &x)` do with your implementation?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```c
void swap(int *a, int *b) { int t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t; }
```
With `int` parameters the function swaps its own copies, invisible to the
caller. `swap(&x, &x)` works: `t = x; x = x; x = t` leaves `x` unchanged. (The
"clever" version without a temporary, `*a ^= *b; *b ^= *a; *a ^= *b;`, sets
`x` to 0 when both pointers are equal — one more reason to prefer clear code.)
:::

::: {#exr-cpp5-overflow}
Using @prp-overflow-test, write a C function `bool parse_u32(const char *s,
uint32_t *out)` that accepts only non-empty strings of decimal digits whose
value fits in `uint32_t`, without calling any library parser and without ever
overflowing.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```c
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdint.h>
bool parse_u32(const char *s, uint32_t *out) {
    const uint32_t M = UINT32_MAX;
    uint32_t v = 0;
    if (*s == '\0') return false;
    for (; *s; ++s) {
        if (*s < '0' || *s > '9') return false;
        uint32_t d = (uint32_t)(*s - '0');
        if (v > (M - d) / 10) return false;      /* 10v + d would exceed M */
        v = 10 * v + d;                          /* safe by the proposition */
    }
    *out = v;
    return true;
}
```
:::

::: {#exr-cpp5-buffer}
A program writes 1 000 000 lines of 20 bytes each to a file. How many `write`
system calls are made with the default 4 096-byte buffer? With a 64 KiB buffer
set by `setvbuf`? And if the program calls `fflush` after every line?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$n = 2\cdot10^7$ bytes. With $B = 4096$: $\lceil 2\cdot10^7/4096\rceil = 4883$
calls. With $B = 65\,536$: $\lceil 2\cdot 10^7 / 65\,536\rceil = 306$ calls.
Flushing after every line defeats the buffer: $10^6$ calls, one per line.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp5-csv}
Encode the fields `a"b`, `,`, an empty field and `x y` with `csv_join`, then
decode the result by hand with the two-state machine of `csv_split`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
`a"b` contains a quote → `"a""b"`; `,` → `","`; the empty field stays empty;
`x y` needs no quotes. The line is `"a""b",",",,x y`. Decoding: `"` at the
start of a field opens quotes; `a`; `""` → one `"`; `b`; `"` closes; `,` ends
field 1 (`a"b`). `"` opens; `,` inside quotes is data; `"` closes; `,` ends
field 2 (`,`). The next `,` ends field 3 (empty). `x y` is field 4. Four
fields, equal to the originals.
:::
